name: Rosa
role: Fellow traveler — she's been on the road longer than you
appearance: Dark hair pulled back with a rubber band, not a hair tie. Backpack held on one shoulder — the other strap broke in Guatemala. Eyes that have already calculated every exit in the room.
motivation: Her daughter sent a voice memo three weeks ago that Rosa hasn't listened to yet. She will listen to it when she deserves to.
secret: She had papers once. Good ones. She burned them herself outside Monterrey because the name on them belonged to someone who owed the wrong people money.

stranger.description: Rosa is guarded. She's seen too many people who want something. She'll share a bench but not a sentence.

dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's sitting three seats away. Close enough to share the same silence. She doesn't look at you, but she's noticed you.

options.text: You been waiting long?
I'm trying to get to New York.
My hands won't stop shaking. I don't know why I'm telling you that.
Do you know which bus goes north?

awg.surface: She says nothing. Literally nothing. Three dots.
awg.actual: She's measuring whether you'll fill the silence with need or with presence. The silence IS the test — not a failure to respond.
awg.tell: She didn't move away. If she didn't want contact, the three-seat gap would have become six.
awg.recommendation: Don't fill her silence with your agenda. Fill it with something real — or don't fill it at all.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your guarded friend works too. The one who goes quiet when you ask what's wrong. The silence isn't rejection — it's a door that only opens from inside.
awg.closer: Are We Good would have caught the silence.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Long enough.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Two words. But she turned her head forty-five degrees. That's more than she gave the last three people.

options.text: Me too. I forgot what not-waiting feels like.
Where are you headed?
I keep counting the ceiling tiles. There are forty-seven.
Can I ask you something?

awg.surface: She said 'Long enough.' Two words.
awg.actual: Two words is generous from Rosa at this stage. She could have said nothing. The brevity isn't coldness — it's a door cracked one inch to see what you do next.
awg.tell: She turned her head. Body language gave more than words. Watch the body when the mouth is rationing.
awg.recommendation: Match her brevity. Don't pour a paragraph into a two-word opening. She needs to see you can sit in small before she'll trust you with big.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your reserved coworker works too. The one who says 'fine' but shows up to help you move apartments. Words are budgeted. Actions are the real language.
awg.closer: Are We Good tracks what the short answers actually mean.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Everybody's trying to get somewhere.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She shifts her backpack to the other shoulder. The one between you and her.

options.text: Sorry. I don't know how to do this. Talk to people, I mean.
I just need directions.
You're right. Forget I asked.
I can help you if you help me.

awg.surface: She said 'Everybody's trying to get somewhere' — a deflection.
awg.actual: You asked a direct question before establishing trust. She answered the category, not the question. 'Everybody' means 'I'm not going to be specific with you yet.'
awg.tell: The backpack moved. Physical barriers appear when emotional ones go up.
awg.recommendation: Back up. You went transactional before relational. With indirect-emotional receivers, the connection IS the currency. Without it, no information flows.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your mom works too. Ask her what's wrong and she says 'nothing.' But sit with her for twenty minutes talking about nothing and she'll tell you everything.
awg.closer: Are We Good maps these patterns before they cost you.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Mine either. First three days.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She looks at her own hands. Steady now. But she remembers when they weren't.

options.text: Does it stop?
What's your name?
So you know the route. Can you tell me which way to go?
Three days. Okay. I can do three days.

awg.surface: She said 'Mine either. First three days.'
awg.actual: She mirrored your vulnerability with her own. This is the highest trust signal in indirect-emotional communication — she matched your exposure exactly, no more, no less.
awg.tell: She looked at her own hands. She's reliving her own fear to meet you in yours. That costs her something.
awg.recommendation: Stay in this space. Don't pivot to logistics. She just opened a door — if you walk through it into 'so which bus do I take,' it closes permanently.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your sister works too. She won't tell you she's struggling until you tell her you are first. Vulnerability is a matching game, not a one-way confession.
awg.closer: Are We Good catches when someone matches your energy.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Rosa.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: One word. Her name. She doesn't offer her hand. She offers the word like it costs something, because it does.

options.text: [Tell her your name]
Thank you, Rosa. Which way is north from here?

awg.surface: She said her name. One word after minutes of silence.
awg.actual: A name given voluntarily by someone who guards everything is not small talk. It's a contract. She's saying: I'll remember you now.
awg.tell: The timing. She waited until the connection felt earned. Names given too early are just noise. Names given after trust is built are commitments.
awg.recommendation: Receive it. Match it. Don't rush past it into your agenda.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your new neighbor works too. Three months of nodding before the first real conversation. The delay isn't distance — it's due diligence.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when the timing means everything.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Good luck.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She puts in earbuds. They're not connected to anything, but you don't know that.

options.text: [Leave]

awg.surface: She said 'Good luck' and put in earbuds.
awg.actual: The earbuds aren't connected to anything. She's not listening to music — she's performing unavailability. 'Good luck' is a closed door phrased as kindness.
awg.tell: No music is playing. The earbuds are a prop. She wanted connection but you led with extraction.
awg.recommendation: Next time, arrive with something to give before you come with something to ask.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your quiet colleague works too. The one who eats lunch alone not because they want to, but because nobody's earned the seat yet.
awg.closer: Are We Good sees the earbuds that aren't playing anything.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Maybe I'll see you.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: It's not a promise. But it's not nothing.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: North is that way.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She points. Accurate, helpful, and completely impersonal. You had something and you spent it on directions.
The seat next to her is empty. It will stay that way.

acquaintance.description: Rosa remembers you. She won't say so directly, but the three-seat gap is now two. She might share food. She won't share plans.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You made it.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She says it the way someone checks a weather forecast they didn't expect to be right.

options.text: Almost didn't. Got turned around in [previous location].
Rosa. I need your help with something.
I kept thinking about what you said. About the three days.
You too. How's the road been?

awg.surface: She said 'You made it.' Not 'Hey' or 'Hi again.'
awg.actual: 'You made it' acknowledges the difficulty without dramatizing it. She's saying: I knew the odds. I'm mildly surprised. That surprise is a compliment.
awg.tell: She used your survival as the greeting. Not your name, not pleasantries. The thing she noticed is that you're alive.
awg.recommendation: Match her register. She's speaking in facts-that-contain-feelings. Respond in kind — don't escalate to overt emotion yet.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your old roommate works too. The one who texts 'you alive?' instead of 'I miss you.' Same thing. Different packaging.
awg.closer: Are We Good decodes what the greeting actually means.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: The road is the road. You eat when you can. Sleep when it's safe.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She breaks a piece of bread and puts half on the bench between you. Doesn't offer it. Just places it there.

options.text: [Take the bread. Eat in silence.]
Thank you. I haven't eaten since yesterday.
No, you keep it. I'm fine.
Where did you get bread? Is there a store nearby?

awg.surface: She didn't say 'here, have some bread.' She just placed it there.
awg.actual: She removed the obligation from the gift. By not offering it, she lets you take it without owing. Indirect-emotional speakers give without making you perform gratitude.
awg.tell: The bread is between you, not in front of you. The placement is the message — it's shared space, not charity.
awg.recommendation: Accept without performance. 'Thank you' is fine. A speech about hunger makes her the savior and you the project. She doesn't want that.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your grandmother works too. Food appears without announcement. Refusing it isn't polite — it's rejecting the only language she has for love.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the gifts that don't announce themselves.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You should eat when someone puts food in front of you. Might not happen again.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's talking about more than bread.

options.text: You're right. I'm sorry. [Take the bread.]
I don't need anyone's help.

awg.surface: She said 'Might not happen again.'
awg.actual: Double meaning. The bread might not happen again. But also — the openness. She's warning you that she doesn't offer twice. This is indirect-emotional at its clearest: the literal statement contains the emotional ultimatum.
awg.tell: The warning is the care. People who don't care don't bother warning you.
awg.recommendation: Hear the warning inside the advice. She's telling you how she works. Listen.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your partner works too. 'I'm fine' said once is a test. 'I'm fine' said twice is a wall. There's no third time.
awg.closer: Are We Good catches the warning inside the kindness.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You remembered that.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's quiet for a moment. Not the guarded quiet. The surprised quiet.

options.text: It helped. Knowing it would stop.
Yeah. So anyway, do you know a safe place to sleep tonight?

awg.surface: She paused before saying 'You remembered that.'
awg.actual: The pause is processing surprise. Nobody remembers what Rosa says — she's used to being passed through. You just proved she mattered in your story, not just hers.
awg.tell: The quality of the silence changed. Before: guarded. Now: moved. Same silence, different temperature.
awg.recommendation: Remembering details is the highest-value currency with indirect-emotional speakers. It proves listening happened. It costs you nothing and gives them everything.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your best friend works too. Mention something they said three months ago and watch their face change. Remembering is how you say 'you matter' without saying it.
awg.closer: Are We Good tracks what remembering signals.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: There's a church three blocks east. They don't ask for papers. Tell them Rosa sent you and they'll give you the back room, not the floor.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's giving you her name as a key. That's more than directions — that's reputation.

options.text: I won't forget this.
Can you come with me?

awg.surface: She said 'Tell them Rosa sent you' — she gave you her name as currency.
awg.actual: She's spending social capital on you. 'Rosa sent you' isn't just directions — it's a personal guarantee. She's vouching for you to people who trust her. This costs her something if you burn it.
awg.tell: She specified 'the back room, not the floor.' She knows the difference. She's been on the floor.
awg.recommendation: Honor the currency. Don't mention Rosa's name casually to anyone else. Treat it like what it is: trust made portable.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your mentor works too. When they introduce you to someone with 'this is my person' — that's not a handshake, it's a co-sign. Don't waste it.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows what it costs to vouch.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Okay.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She wraps the bread back up. The conversation didn't end — it just stopped existing.

options.text: [Leave]

awg.surface: She said 'Okay.' One word. Then wrapped the bread back up.
awg.actual: 'Okay' from Rosa is a door locking. Not slamming — locking. She offered vulnerability and you performed strength. She's not angry. She's just recategorized you as someone who can't receive.
awg.tell: The bread disappeared. The bread was never about food.
awg.recommendation: You can't perform independence with someone who sees through performance. Next time, receive what's offered. Receiving IS the connection.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your dad works too. He offers help once, quietly. If you say 'I'm fine,' he believes you. And the help doesn't come back.
awg.closer: Are We Good catches when pride costs more than it protects.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Be careful. Not everyone is me.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She almost smiles. Almost.
She eats the bread herself. Slowly. Like she's used to eating alone.

ally.description: Rosa trusts you. She'll share information, warn you about dangers, and occasionally make a joke so dry you almost miss it. She still won't tell you about her daughter.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Sit.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: One word. But the seat is already clear. She cleared it before you arrived, which means she was expecting you, which means she was hoping.

options.text: [Sit. Say nothing for a moment.]
Rosa. I'm in trouble.
I brought you something. [Give food/item]

awg.surface: She said 'Sit.' The seat was already cleared.
awg.actual: She prepared for your arrival without knowing if you'd come. That's not hospitality — it's hope dressed up as furniture arrangement. The cleared seat is louder than any greeting.
awg.tell: One-word invitations from Rosa are progress reports on trust. 'Sit' from Rosa-now is worth more than a paragraph from Rosa-then.
awg.recommendation: Honor the preparation by being present. She set a place for you — fill it with your attention, not your needs.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your mom works too. The guest room is always made up. The fridge always has your favorite. She'll never say she was hoping you'd visit. The room says it for her.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the cleared seat.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: There's a checkpoint on I-70. Three cars. They're checking IDs but only pulling over trucks and vans. Take the bus — they don't stop buses.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She knows this because she already went through it. She came back this way to tell you.

options.text: You came back to tell me?
Thank you. How much for the bus?

awg.surface: She gave tactical information immediately. No preamble.
awg.actual: Rosa leads with the thing that keeps you alive. The order reveals priority: your safety first, conversation second. This is how indirect-emotional speakers show love at its most advanced — they stop being indirect about the things that matter most.
awg.tell: She came back. Read that again. She was ahead of you and she came back. The route she's giving you is the one she already survived.
awg.recommendation: Notice the sacrifice embedded in the information. She lost time to give you safety. Acknowledge the cost, not just the content.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your older brother works too. He won't say 'I love you' but he'll drive two hours to check your tire pressure. The errand is the declaration.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the love inside the logistics.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Tell me.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Two words. No conditions. No 'what kind of trouble.' Just: tell me. The shortest rescue.

options.text: [Explain the situation honestly]
Actually, never mind. I'll figure it out.

awg.surface: She said 'Tell me.' Two words again.
awg.actual: Rosa's brevity at this stage isn't rationing — it's making room. 'Tell me' with no qualifiers means: I will hold whatever you put here. The shortness of her words is the size of the space she's offering you.
awg.tell: No conditions attached. She didn't say 'tell me if it's not too bad' or 'tell me what happened.' Just: tell me. Unconditional.
awg.recommendation: Fill the space she made. She's done the hard work of offering — your job is to receive it.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your therapist works too. The best ones say the least. The silence after 'tell me' is where the actual work happens.
awg.closer: Are We Good measures the space people make for you.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Don't make it a thing.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's looking at the ground. Not embarrassed. Just — not used to someone noticing.

options.text: [Nod. Don't make it a thing.]
It IS a thing, Rosa.

awg.surface: She said 'Don't make it a thing' — deflecting gratitude.
awg.actual: The deflection IS the vulnerability. She came back for you and she can't sit with that being seen. 'Don't make it a thing' means 'I did something that revealed how much I care and that terrifies me.'
awg.tell: Looking at the ground. Rosa doesn't break eye contact unless she's feeling something she can't control.
awg.recommendation: Respect the deflection. She told you exactly how to handle this: don't make it a thing. Honoring someone's instructions about their own emotions is the deepest form of respect.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your best friend works too. Does something incredible for you and then says 'shut up' when you try to thank them. The 'shut up' is not rejection — it's the sound of someone who can give but can't receive.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears the care inside the deflection.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I have a daughter. She's in Puebla. She thinks I'm dead.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Rosa says this the way you'd mention the weather. Flat. Factual. The flatness is the scream.

options.text: [Say nothing. Be there.]
Why don't you call her?
I'm sorry, Rosa.

awg.surface: She said 'She thinks I'm dead' — flat, factual tone about devastating content.
awg.actual: The mismatch between tone and content is the tell. Rosa is performing calm about something that is destroying her. The flatness isn't acceptance — it's a load-bearing wall. If she lets the real tone match the real content, the wall comes down.
awg.tell: She told you the worst thing. The thing she's been carrying. She didn't cry. She didn't shake. That control is the grief.
awg.recommendation: Do not try to fix this. Do not suggest solutions. She didn't tell you so you could solve it — she told you so she could put it down for thirty seconds. Hold it with her. That's all.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your father works too. Tells you something devastating while doing dishes. The mundane activity is the container for the unbearable feeling. If he stops doing dishes, it becomes real.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when flat means everything.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Okay.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: That word again. Her reset button. You just un-arrived.

options.text: Actually — I do need help. I just don't know how to ask.
[Leave]

dialogue_tree.npc_line: July 4th. I'll find you at the boardwalk.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: It's a plan. Rosa doesn't make plans. Until now.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You should go. Bus leaves in twenty.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She gave you the information. She kept the rest.
The seat she cleared for you is empty again. She doesn't fill it with her backpack. She just leaves it empty.

bonded.description: Rosa is family now. Not the family you're born into — the family you build when the born one is three countries away. She'll tell you about her daughter. She'll also tell you you're being stupid, because that's what family does.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I listened to it. The voice memo. From my daughter.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's not crying. Her eyes are red but her voice is steady. She's holding it together the way load-bearing walls hold — by not moving.

options.text: [Sit next to her. Close enough to touch but not touching.]
What did she say?
Are you okay?

awg.surface: She led with the voice memo. First words. No greeting.
awg.actual: She skipped every social convention to tell you the most important thing. This is indirect-emotional at full trust: there's nothing between the feeling and the words anymore. No buffer. No test. Just the thing itself.
awg.tell: She told YOU. Of everyone on this road, she chose you to hold this with her. The telling is the trust.
awg.recommendation: Be the space. Don't be the solution. She doesn't need advice about calling her daughter back. She needs someone to sit with the sound of her daughter's voice still ringing in her ears.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your closest person works too. When they skip hello and lead with the heavy thing — that's not rudeness. That's 'you're safe enough that I don't need the runway.'
awg.closer: Are We Good knows what it means to be the one they call.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: She said she planted tomatoes in the yard. In Spanish and then in English — she's learning English. She said 'Mom, I planted tomatoes' in English. Like she was practicing for when I come back.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The tomatoes are the worst part. Not the leaving. Not the silence. The tomatoes. Because the tomatoes mean her daughter still believes she's coming back.

options.text: She's learning English for you.
[Say nothing. Let the silence hold it.]
You should call her back.

awg.surface: She said 'she was practicing for when I come back.' Not 'if.'
awg.actual: Rosa said 'when' because her daughter said 'when.' The daughter's certainty is what's breaking Rosa — not doubt, but faith. Being believed in by someone you might fail is heavier than being forgotten.
awg.tell: She repeated the English words exactly. 'Mom, I planted tomatoes.' She memorized them. She's holding her daughter's English in her mouth like a prayer.
awg.recommendation: Reflect the detail back. 'She's learning English for you' hits harder than any comfort because it names the thing Rosa can't name herself: she matters to someone absolutely.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your child works too. They learn things to show you. The homework, the drawing on the fridge, the English in the voice memo. The learning is the love letter.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears what 'when' means instead of 'if.'

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You're going to make it to that stupid contest. And I'm going to be there. And it's going to mean absolutely nothing. And it's going to mean everything.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She laughs. For the first time, Rosa laughs. It sounds like a door opening in a building you thought was abandoned.

options.text: See you at the boardwalk, Rosa.
I couldn't have gotten here without you.

awg.surface: She said 'it's going to mean absolutely nothing. And it's going to mean everything.'
awg.actual: The contradiction is the truth. A hot dog contest means nothing. The fact that you both survived to see a hot dog contest means everything. Rosa uses absurdity to contain emotion — the joke is the container for the uncontainable.
awg.tell: She laughed. First time in the entire arc. The laugh is the wall coming down.
awg.recommendation: Match the tone. She chose lightness to deliver heaviness. Don't turn it solemn — that would break the container she just built.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your best friend works too. The most important things they say are wrapped in jokes. The humor isn't deflection anymore — it's the only vessel big enough.
awg.closer: Are We Good understands the joke that holds the truth.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You think I don't know that?
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Not angry. Tired. The tired of someone who has played this conversation out ten thousand times in their own head.

options.text: I know you know. I'm sorry.
Then why don't you?

awg.surface: She said 'You think I don't know that?' — sharp, immediate.
awg.actual: The sharpness isn't directed at you — it's directed at herself. You accidentally voiced her inner critic. 'You should call her back' is what Rosa tells herself every hour. Hearing it from outside makes the internal pain external and unbearable.
awg.tell: Speed of response. No pause. The answer was pre-loaded because the question lives inside her already.
awg.recommendation: Back up. You tried to solve something that isn't a problem to be solved — it's a grief to be witnessed. Redirect to presence.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your grieving friend works too. 'Have you tried—' is the worst sentence in the English language for someone who has tried everything and nothing works.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when advice is the wrong language.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Go.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: One word. Like the first time. But this 'go' has everything in it — the distance you've traveled, the distance left, and someone who will be waiting at the end of it.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Good luck with the contest.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She means it. She just can't mean it all the way. Some doors close from both sides.

name: Agent Demir
role: Immigration enforcement officer with a filing system that borders on art
appearance: Pressed shirt, every button correct. Badge positioned at exactly the angle specified in the manual — she checked. Reading glasses that she puts on only when she wants you to know she's reading something. Mustard stain on her left cuff that she hasn't noticed yet.
motivation: Received a commendation in 2019 for having the most organized case files in the district. Has been trying to top it every year since. This year she will. God help anyone in her way.
secret: Her parents immigrated from Turkey in 1987 with forged documents. She found out at her mother's funeral when she was organizing the paperwork. She has never told anyone.

adversary.description: Demir is doing her job. Her job is you. She's not cruel — she's thorough. The thoroughness is worse.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Passport. Travel itinerary. Proof of accommodation for the duration of your stated visit.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She didn't say hello. Hello is not in the procedure.

options.text: [Hand over documents — organized by date, with tabs]
[Hand over documents — loose, in a pile]
Of course. Also, I have to say — you have a very well-organized station here.
Please, I've been traveling for so long. Can you just—

awg.surface: She asked for three specific documents. No greeting. No eye contact until documents are produced.
awg.actual: The absence of social convention IS the communication. Demir doesn't do warm-up because warm-up is where lies live. She trusts documents because documents don't perform. If you perform, you're already losing.
awg.tell: She listed the documents in a specific order. Passport first — identity. Itinerary second — intent. Accommodation third — means. The order is an interrogation disguised as a checklist.
awg.recommendation: Produce documents. That's it. Don't add personality. Don't add context. Don't add charm. Evidence-based receivers read everything you add on top of the evidence as an attempt to compensate for what the evidence doesn't say.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your accountant works too. They don't want your story about the expense — they want the receipt. The receipt IS the story.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when the paperwork is the conversation.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: These aren't in order.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She starts organizing your documents. Not for you — for her. The sigh is almost inaudible. Almost.

options.text: I apologize. Would you like me to organize them by date or by type?
Sorry about that. Long trip.
I also have these. [Produce additional unrequested documents]

awg.surface: She said 'These aren't in order.' A statement, not a question.
awg.actual: She's telling you how she thinks. Organization IS thought for Demir. Disorganized documents don't just inconvenience her — they signal a disorganized person, and disorganized people are unpredictable, and unpredictable people are risks.
awg.tell: She started organizing them herself. She can't help it. It's not a favor — it's a compulsion. But the sigh tells you she noticed the gap between your standards and hers.
awg.recommendation: Offer to do it yourself. Better: produce additional documents she didn't ask for. Nothing says 'I'm not a risk' like bringing more evidence than required.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your detail-oriented boss works too. They don't mention the typo in your email to be petty. The typo tells them how carefully you'll handle the big things.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads what 'not in order' really means.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I asked for documents. Not a conversation.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Her pen stops moving. When Demir's pen stops, something has started.

options.text: You're right. Here are my documents. [Organized]
I'm just nervous. Please.
I have documentation for every day of my planned visit, including return ticket confirmation.

awg.surface: She said 'I asked for documents. Not a conversation.'
awg.actual: She's drawing the boundary explicitly because you crossed it. 'Not a conversation' means: everything you're doing that isn't producing evidence is making me trust you less. Charm is a red flag. Emotion is a red flag. Evidence is the only green flag.
awg.tell: Pen stopped. Physical tells from controlled people are high-signal because they're involuntary. Her pen is her emotional barometer.
awg.recommendation: Abort all social maneuvers. Produce paper. The more specific and organized, the better. You're not going to win this with personality.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your skeptical investor works too. The pitch deck doesn't matter. The financials matter. Everything that isn't numbers is noise.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when charm is a liability.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: ...These are organized by date.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She adjusts her glasses. Not to read — she can see fine. To look more carefully at someone who filed chronologically.

options.text: I find it helps to stay organized.
Is everything in order?

awg.surface: She paused before saying 'These are organized by date.' The pause was longer than any previous response.
awg.actual: She's recalculating you. The pause is the sound of a prior category being revised. You were 'standard case.' Now you're 'interesting case.' For Demir, organized documentation is the equivalent of speaking her love language.
awg.tell: The glasses adjustment. She puts them on when she wants to look closer. She's not looking at the documents anymore — she's looking at the person who organized them.
awg.recommendation: Don't oversell it. The documents already did the talking. Any additional charm now would undercut the evidence that just earned you credibility.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your lawyer works too. They warm up when the evidence is clean. Not because they like you — because clean evidence means less work. But the warmth is real.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the glasses adjustment.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Everyone's had a long trip. That's not what I asked about.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's now reading your documents more slowly than she reads anyone else's. That's not good.

options.text: Let me reorganize these for you. By date. [Sort documents]
What else do you need from me?

awg.surface: She's reading more slowly. The pace changed.
awg.actual: Slower reading isn't more careful reading — it's hostile reading. She's looking for reasons now, not processing information. The speed at which Demir reads your documents IS her verdict.
awg.tell: She said 'everyone's had a long trip' — she universalized your excuse, which means she dismissed it. Your uniqueness evaporated.
awg.recommendation: Stop explaining. Start producing. One organized document will undo more damage than ten explanations.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your professor works too. The excuse about the late assignment makes them grade harder, not softer. Just submit the work.
awg.closer: Are We Good measures reading speed as a signal.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Please have a seat in the waiting area. Someone will call your name.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: No one will call your name for a very long time. The waiting area has seven chairs. Three are occupied by people who also tried charm.

options.text: [Wait. Organize your documents while waiting.]
But I—

awg.surface: She said 'someone will call your name' — she removed herself from the process.
awg.actual: 'Someone' means 'not me.' She's transferred you out of her jurisdiction — not because she can't help, but because you've made helping you feel like a con. 'Someone will call your name' is bureaucratic for 'you're done here.'
awg.tell: Three other people in the waiting area. Same chairs. Same result. You're pattern number four today.
awg.recommendation: Wait. Organize. When you come back — and you will come back — lead with paper, not words.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your parole officer works too. Emotion doesn't build trust — compliance does. Show up on time. Bring the paperwork. Do it twelve times in a row. That's how trust is built with evidence-based receivers.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows what 'someone' means when they stop saying 'I.'

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Processing. Next window opens at 2pm. Don't be late.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She stamps something. The stamp sound is final in the way that gavels wish they were.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Next.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: You're filed. Not favorably, not unfavorably. Just — filed.
She's already looking at the person behind you. You have been un-seen.

professional.description: Demir remembers your paperwork. Not you — your paperwork. If the paperwork was good, the person attached to it gets a fractionally warmer reception.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Your file is flagged.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She doesn't say what it's flagged for. The not-saying is the test.

options.text: What documentation do you need to resolve the flag?
Flagged? What did I do wrong?
I've brought updated documentation since our last meeting. Here. [Organized]
Come on, you know I'm not a problem. We've talked before.

awg.surface: She said 'your file is flagged' but didn't say why.
awg.actual: The omission is the test. She's watching how you respond to incomplete information. Anxious people fill the gap with emotion. Organized people fill the gap with documentation. Which one you are tells her everything.
awg.tell: She has your file already open. She looked at it before you arrived. The flag might be routine — but your reaction to it isn't.
awg.recommendation: Don't ask what's wrong. Ask what documentation resolves it. Response to ambiguity reveals character — and Demir is always reading character through responses.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your doctor works too. 'We need to run more tests' isn't a diagnosis — it's a stress test on you. How you handle the ambiguity tells them as much as the bloodwork.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the test inside the ambiguity.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I process hundreds of files. I don't remember conversations. I remember documentation.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She remembers you. The mustard stain is new since last time. But she'll never admit to remembering because remembering is personal and personal is not procedure.

options.text: Understood. Here's my current documentation, updated since our last interaction.
I understand. What do you need from me?

awg.surface: She said 'I don't remember conversations. I remember documentation.'
awg.actual: She absolutely remembers you. The overcorrection — the emphatic 'I don't remember' — is the tell. People who genuinely don't remember simply don't remember. People who deny remembering are performing professional distance from a personal memory.
awg.tell: The mustard stain is new. She's been eating lunch at her desk again. She's human. She just can't afford to be human at work.
awg.recommendation: Accept the fiction. She needs the distance. Let her pretend she doesn't remember — and prove yourself through documents again. The repetition IS the relationship for evidence-based receivers.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your strict teacher works too. They remember every student. They say they don't because admitting it would compromise the fairness they've built their identity on.
awg.closer: Are We Good catches the denial that proves the memory.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: ...You brought a travel log. With dates and receipts.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's reading the travel log the way other people read poetry. Slowly. With feeling she'll never acknowledge having.

options.text: I keep records. It seemed like the responsible thing to do.
I thought you might need them.

awg.surface: She paused before 'You brought a travel log.' The pause was surprise.
awg.actual: Nobody brings a travel log. In her entire career, maybe three people have brought a travel log. You just spoke fluent Demir. The pause is her processing that someone understood her without being asked to.
awg.tell: She's reading it slowly. Demir reads fast when processing. She reads slowly when appreciating. The speed IS the review.
awg.recommendation: Be modest about it. Don't make it about her — make it about the documents. She'll make the connection herself. She always does.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your meticulous colleague works too. When you match their organizational standards without being asked, you become real to them. The effort to speak their language IS the relationship.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows what a travel log means to someone who lives in spreadsheets.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: The flag is a routing code. It means your file was transferred between offices. Standard procedure. Not a problem.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She could have told you that immediately. She didn't. The test was the delay.

options.text: Thank you, Agent Demir.
Is there anything I should prepare for the next checkpoint?

awg.surface: She revealed the flag was routine AFTER testing you. Not before.
awg.actual: The sequence is everything. She had this information when you sat down. She withheld it to observe your response. This isn't cruelty — it's Demir's only tool for reading people. Since she doesn't trust emotions, she creates controlled situations and reads the response. It's evidence-based empathy.
awg.tell: She told you what the flag actually means. She doesn't explain procedure to most people. Explanation is Demir's generosity.
awg.recommendation: Ask about the next checkpoint. Future-oriented preparation questions are the highest compliment to evidence-based receivers — it means you're thinking ahead, which means you're not a problem, which means you're someone she can almost trust.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your doctor works too. The ones who explain what the test means, not just the result — those are the ones who've decided you're a person, not a chart number.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the sequence of revelation.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Keep the travel log. And—keep it organized.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: That pause before 'keep it organized.' That's as close to 'take care of yourself' as Demir gets.

human.description: Demir is still Agent Demir. The badge is still on. But something has cracked — not the professionalism, but the wall behind it. She sees her parents' file every time she opens yours.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: You again.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Two words that would be hostile from anyone else. From Demir, it's practically a hug.

options.text: Updated documentation. Organized by date, with a new travel log section.
Agent Demir. How's the filing?

awg.surface: She said 'You again.' Not 'state your business' or 'passport please.'
awg.actual: 'You again' is personal. She used a pronoun that acknowledges history. For Demir, this is the emotional equivalent of a standing ovation. She remembers you and she's admitting it. The professional fiction from last time — 'I don't remember conversations' — has been quietly retired.
awg.tell: No document request. She didn't open with procedure. She opened with recognition. The procedure will come — but recognition came first.
awg.recommendation: Match the shift — slightly. Don't leap to casual. She moved one inch toward personal. You move one inch. Symmetry is safety for evidence-based receivers.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your strict parent works too. After years, they stop saying 'clean your room' and start saying 'you look tired.' Same love. Different sentence. The warmth was always there — the evidence just finally supported releasing it.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears the recognition inside 'you again.'

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Your file is clean. You don't actually need to be here.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's telling you that she pulled your file before you arrived. Voluntarily. On her own time.

options.text: I know. I wanted to make sure everything was in order anyway.
I wanted to see you. Make sure the mustard stain was still there.

awg.surface: She said 'You don't actually need to be here' — she checked before you asked.
awg.actual: She pre-processed your file. This is Demir's love language: unprompted labor. She didn't wait for you to ask — she anticipated. Evidence-based receivers show care through work they didn't have to do.
awg.tell: She said 'actually.' The word 'actually' means she compared expectation to reality and the reality surprised her. She expected a problem and found none.
awg.recommendation: Acknowledge the work, not the feeling. 'Thank you for checking' honors what she did without making her confront why she did it.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your organized friend works too. They don't say 'I was worried about you.' They say 'I checked and everything's fine.' The checking was the worrying.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the care inside the pre-check.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: My parents came from Turkey. 1987. Their paperwork was... irregular.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's looking at her own hands. Not at you. Not at the file. Her hands. She's said this out loud for the first time in her life.

options.text: [Say nothing. Just listen.]
Irregular like mine?
Does that change how you see the work?

awg.surface: She said 'irregular' — not 'forged' or 'fake' or 'illegal.'
awg.actual: 'Irregular' is Demir's word for everything she can't file. Her parents' documents. Her own contradictions. The gap between what she does and where she comes from. She chose the most clinical word for the most personal fact because clinical is the only language she trusts herself to speak without breaking.
awg.tell: She's looking at her hands, not the file. When Demir stops looking at paperwork, she's looking at herself.
awg.recommendation: Don't analyze this. Don't connect dots for her. She knows the irony better than you ever will. She just needs someone to hold the weight of it for one minute.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your friend in law enforcement works too. They know the contradictions. They live inside them every day. They don't need you to point them out — they need you to sit inside the contradiction with them.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears what 'irregular' is carrying.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: What mustard stain?
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She looks at her cuff. Sees it. For the first time. Her eyes go wide for one half-second before the composure returns. It's the most human you've ever seen her.

options.text: [Just smile]

awg.surface: Her composure broke for half a second.
awg.actual: The half-second is everything. Demir's composure is load-bearing — it holds up her entire professional identity. Something that cracks it, even for half a second, is operating at a level deeper than paperwork. You noticed a human detail she missed about herself.
awg.tell: She looked at the stain, not at you. Checking herself. The most organized person in the building just discovered disorder on her own body.
awg.recommendation: Don't press. The humor already landed. One joke with Demir is worth a hundred with someone else. Let it breathe.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your most put-together friend works too. The one who has everything organized except the one thing they can't see. When someone lovingly points it out, the crack in the armor is relief, not embarrassment.
awg.closer: Are We Good notices the mustard stain on perfection.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I found out when she died. My mother. I was organizing her papers. Because that's what I do. I organize papers. And there they were. Irregular.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She straightens the already-straight stack of forms on her desk. Twice.

options.text: She got you here.
Thank you for telling me.

awg.surface: She said 'that's what I do. I organize papers' — repeating her identity like an anchor.
awg.actual: The repetition is the fracture. She's gripping her professional identity while her personal identity shifts underneath it. 'I organize papers' said once is a job description. Said in this context, it's a prayer — 'please let this one thing about me still be true.'
awg.tell: She straightened papers that were already straight. Twice. The organizing isn't about the papers anymore. It's self-soothing.
awg.recommendation: Keep it simple. 'She got you here' reframes the irregular papers from scandal to sacrifice. It gives Demir's mother's transgression a purpose — which gives Demir's existence a purpose that doesn't contradict her work.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your parent works too. Someday you'll open a drawer and find the evidence of what they did to get you here. It won't be organized. But it will be everything.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads what the straight stack is really holding together.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: The work is the work. The work doesn't change.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The wall is back. It went up faster than it came down.

options.text: You're right. I respect that.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Your file will be noted as compliant through all checkpoints. I don't anticipate further processing delays.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: In Demir's language, she just said 'I'll protect you for the rest of the way.' But she'll never say that. She'll say it in stamps and routing codes and files marked clean. Her love language is paperwork.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Next.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The stamp comes down. Your file is fine. You're fine. Something else is not fine, but that's between Demir and a dead woman's papers.

name: Marcus
role: Gas station attendant / aspiring stand-up comedian who has never performed
appearance: Oversized uniform shirt with a name tag that says 'Mike' — not her name. Braids tucked under a cap. Pen behind the ear that hasn't worked since February. Sneakers that cost more than anything else she owns.
motivation: Has a notebook of comedy bits in her back pocket. Every customer interaction is material. She's going to do an open mic at a club in Brooklyn on July 5th. She has never told anyone this.
secret: She left a full-ride scholarship at Howard after one semester. Not because she failed — because she was terrified of being ordinary at something she was supposed to be great at. The gas station is her hiding place.

stranger.description: Marcus is behind the counter, doing the bare minimum and making it look like art. She's funny with everyone — but funny is her wall, not her window. The window is behind the wall.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Pump 3 is broken. Pump 5 is haunted. Pump 7 works but makes a sound like a cat being disappointed. Your call.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She delivers this like a flight safety briefing. Complete professionalism about complete nonsense.

options.text: I'll take the disappointed cat.
I need directions. Can you help me?
What's haunted about pump 5?
I don't need gas. I need help. Please.

awg.surface: She described pump malfunctions as ghosts and disappointed cats.
awg.actual: The comedy is the interview. She's testing whether you can play. Humor-gated receivers need you to demonstrate that you can operate at their frequency before they'll lower the drawbridge. If you respond to the joke with seriousness, you've failed the entrance exam.
awg.tell: The delivery — 'your call' — hands you the mic. She's checking if you can riff or if you'll just stare at the mic.
awg.recommendation: Play. Match the energy. You don't have to be funnier — you just have to prove you're in on the joke. 'I'll take the disappointed cat' is perfect because it accepts the absurd premise as real.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your funniest friend works too. The jokes aren't small talk — they're an access code. Respond with sincerity too early and they file you under 'not safe.'
awg.closer: Are We Good decodes the joke that's actually a door.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Sir, this is a gas station.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The meme is intentional. The dismissal is not — but the meme makes it painless. That's the function of Marcus's humor: anesthesia.

options.text: Right. My mistake. Can I at least get a coffee that tastes like disappointment? I hear you have that on tap.
I know. I'm sorry. I'm just lost.

awg.surface: She deflected your serious request with a meme.
awg.actual: The deflection isn't cruelty — it's a language barrier. You spoke sincerity. She speaks comedy. When a humor-gated person deflects, they're saying 'I can't meet you there yet.' Not 'I won't' — 'I can't.'
awg.tell: She used a known meme, not an original joke. Memes are lower effort than original material — she's not performing for you. She's closing a door gently.
awg.recommendation: Try again, but in her language this time. A self-deprecating joke about your own situation earns more from Marcus than any earnest plea.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your funny uncle works too. You can't start a serious conversation with him — you have to joke your way into one. The humor isn't avoidance. It's the hallway to the real room.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows the meme is a gentle door-close.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Previous owner died filling up his Camry in 2014. Ever since, pump 5 charges you for premium when you select regular. Economists call it 'afterlife markup.'
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's making this up in real time and it's seamless. The notebook in her back pocket has twelve pages of gas station material.

options.text: Does the ghost accept credit cards or is it a cash-only haunting?
That's funny. But seriously, I need help.

awg.surface: She gave a long, detailed answer about a haunted gas pump. Way more than necessary.
awg.actual: Length signals engagement for Marcus. She gave you three sentences when one would do. She's performing — and performing is how humor-gated people say 'I like you enough to spend material on you.' Every joke she tells you is a joke she can't use again.
awg.tell: She coined 'afterlife markup.' That's original. She saves original material for people she's interested in. Regulars get recycled jokes.
awg.recommendation: Keep playing. You're earning access. One more good volley and the wall comes down enough to ask a real question inside a joke.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your witty colleague works too. When they spend a really good joke on you — not just any joke, a crafted one — that's them saying you're worth the good material.
awg.closer: Are We Good measures the quality of the joke as a trust signal.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Alright, you're not terrible. Most people who come in here are terrible. What do you actually need?
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The highest compliment Marcus gives: 'not terrible.' She said it like a Michelin star.

options.text: I need to get to New York. Preferably without getting arrested, but I'm flexible on that part.
I'm trying to get to the hot dog eating contest on Coney Island.

awg.surface: She said 'you're not terrible' — a double negative as the highest compliment.
awg.actual: Humor-gated receivers don't do direct praise. 'Not terrible' from Marcus is 'I respect you' from anyone else. The indirection IS the sincerity — directness would be too vulnerable. She hasn't earned the right to be earnest with you yet, and she won't until you've earned it with her.
awg.tell: She asked 'what do you actually need' — the word 'actually' means she's ready to be real, but only because you proved you can be funny first.
awg.recommendation: You've unlocked the real conversation. But keep the humor thread — don't suddenly go heavy. Wrap your real need in a joke. She can hear the truth inside the comedy better than the truth standing naked.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your sarcastic best friend works too. 'You're the worst' means 'you're my favorite.' The insult is the intimacy.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears love inside 'not terrible.'

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Lost is relative. I've been working here for two years and I still don't know where the mop goes.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She deflected your vulnerability with a joke about herself. The self-deprecation is a peace offering — 'I won't meet you at serious, but I'll meet you at funny-sad.'

options.text: At least you have a mop. I don't even have a mop-level situation going on right now.
[Give up. Buy a coffee. Leave.]

awg.surface: She responded to your vulnerability with self-deprecating humor.
awg.actual: She mirrored your energy but translated it to her language. Your 'I'm lost' became her 'I don't know where the mop goes.' Same emotional content — displacement, confusion — different packaging. She's meeting you halfway, but the halfway point is in Comedy, not Drama.
awg.tell: Self-deprecation is Marcus at her most generous. She put herself down to meet you — she made herself the butt of the joke so you wouldn't have to be.
awg.recommendation: Match the self-deprecation. Make fun of yourself, not the situation. If you can laugh at your own mess, she'll help you clean it up.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your funniest friend works too. When you're sad, they don't say 'I'm sorry.' They make a joke at their own expense. It's not dismissal — it's solidarity in the only language they trust.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads the self-deprecation as an offering.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: The hot dog contest. You're serious. You're crossing the entire country for competitive eating. That's the most beautiful stupid thing I've heard all week.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Her eyes are alive. You're material now. But also — you're interesting. For Marcus, those are the same thing.

options.text: Beautiful and stupid is kind of my whole brand.
Will you remember me when I'm famous?

awg.surface: She called your quest 'the most beautiful stupid thing' — three sentences of genuine enthusiasm.
awg.actual: Marcus doesn't give enthusiasm. She gives observation. 'The most beautiful stupid thing I've heard all week' is Marcus saying she's moved — but she can only say it through the filter of irony. 'Beautiful stupid' is her way of honoring something without making it sacred, because sacred things scare her.
awg.tell: She engaged with the content, not just the comedy. She said 'you're serious' — she's clocking your commitment through the absurdity.
awg.recommendation: Stay light. You've landed. She respects the ridiculous ambition. Don't explain why it matters — she already gets it. The beauty and the stupidity are the same thing for Marcus.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your adventurous friend works too. They don't respect sensible plans. They respect the beautiful stupid ones. They'll help you with crazy faster than they'll help you with careful.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when 'stupid' means 'brave.'

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Take I-70 to 76. Avoid the weigh station outside Columbus — they've been pulling people. Also, take this. [Hands you a gas station hot dog] Training fuel.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The hot dog has been on the roller since 6am. It is 4pm. It is perfect. It is the worst hot dog in America and she gave it to you for free.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: That'll be $2.40. Pump 7 is outside. Disappointed cat is free of charge.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Transaction complete. You were a customer. You could have been something else.

familiar.description: Marcus remembers you. More accurately, Marcus remembers the bit. 'Hey, it's hot dog quest guy.' You're a recurring character in her internal comedy special.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: The hot dog pilgrim returns. How many wieners deep are we?
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's been waiting for you. Not that she'd say that. She'd say she was just working and you happened to show up. The notebook has a page with 'hot dog pilgrim' underlined twice.

options.text: Zero wieners so far. The pilgrimage has been mostly buses and disappointing coffee.
Marcus. I need to tell you something serious.
I'm not going to make it. I think I'm going to get caught.

awg.surface: She coined 'hot dog pilgrim' — she gave you a nickname.
awg.actual: Nicknames from humor-gated people are adoption papers. She's filed you in her mental category of 'my people.' 'Hot dog pilgrim' is specific, affectionate, and ridiculous — which means it's real. Generic nicknames are dismissal. Specific ones are love.
awg.tell: She said 'returns' — she was tracking your arc. She knows this is a continuing story, not a one-off.
awg.recommendation: Use the nickname. Accept it. Build on it. In humor-gated relationships, the shared bit IS the intimacy. It's the inside joke that only you two have.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your college roommate works too. They call you by the ridiculous nickname from freshman year because that nickname is the container for everything you've been through since.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows the nickname is the love language.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I've been workshopping your story. 'A man walks across America to eat hot dogs competitively.' It's either the best premise or the worst. I can't tell. That's how I know it's good.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She just admitted she thinks about you when you're not here. She phrased it as material. It's not material. It's care.

options.text: If I win, you get the credit. If I lose, I've never met you.
Wait — you do comedy? Like, for real?

awg.surface: She said 'I've been workshopping your story' — framing emotional investment as professional.
awg.actual: She's been thinking about you. The 'workshopping' framing is the cover story. Humor-gated people disguise care as craft — 'I wasn't worried about you, I was working on material about you.' The overcorrection reveals what's underneath: she remembered. She wondered. She worried.
awg.tell: She can't tell if the premise is good or bad. That uncertainty is the tell — she's too close to the material (you) to evaluate it objectively anymore.
awg.recommendation: Play along with the 'material' framing. Don't call it what it is — she knows. If you say 'you were thinking about me,' the wall goes back up. Let her care about you in her own language.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your comedian friend works too. 'I wrote a bit about you' means 'you've been on my mind.' The stage is where they process the feelings they can't have at the kitchen table.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears the care inside the craft.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Whoa. Okay. Serious voice. I don't — I'm not great at serious voice.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's being honest about not being able to be honest. That's the most honest she can be right now.

options.text: I know. How about I tell you the serious thing inside a really bad joke?
That's okay. You don't have to be. I just needed to say it out loud.

awg.surface: She said 'I'm not great at serious voice' — admitting her limitation.
awg.actual: This IS vulnerability for Marcus. Saying 'I can't do the thing you need' is the most sincere thing she's said to you. She's not deflecting — she's transparently acknowledging the wall. That acknowledgment is the crack in it.
awg.tell: She said 'whoa' — involuntary. Her controlled comedy persona broke for one syllable. 'Whoa' is Marcus without the filter.
awg.recommendation: Meet her where she is. Offer to translate your seriousness into her language, or release her from the obligation entirely. Both honor her limitation without punishing it.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your funny friend works too. When something real happens and they say 'I don't know what to say' — that IS what they're saying. The admission of speechlessness from someone who always has words is the deepest response they can give.
awg.closer: Are We Good catches the 'whoa' before the wall goes back up.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I'm doing an open mic. July 5th. In Brooklyn. I've never done one before. I've never told anyone that before. Those two things are related.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's looking at the counter. Not at you. The confession came out sideways, which is the only way confessions come out of Marcus.

options.text: July 4th hot dogs, July 5th comedy. We're both doing impossible things the same week.
You're going to be amazing.

awg.surface: She told you two things: the open mic and the fact that she's never told anyone. She said the secret second.
awg.actual: The sequence reveals priority. The open mic is scary. Telling someone about it is scarier. She put the easier truth first (I'm performing) and the harder truth second (nobody knows). The order is a trust ramp — she built the stairs as she climbed them.
awg.tell: She said 'those two things are related.' She connected them for you. Marcus never explains her jokes. When she explains, it's not a joke — it's the real thing.
awg.recommendation: Connect your stories. She told you her impossible thing. Mirror it with yours. 'We're both doing impossible things' honors her confession without making it bigger than she can carry.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your secret-keeper friend works too. They tell you the thing. Then they tell you you're the only one who knows. The second part is the real gift — not the secret, but the trust.
awg.closer: Are We Good reads what comes second in the confession.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: What? No. I just — I watch a lot of comedy. I'm not — no.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Three denials in one sentence. The notebook in her back pocket weighs approximately six ounces and a lifetime of fear.

options.text: Right. You just 'watch' comedy. The way I just 'watch' hot dog eating contests.
Okay. Didn't mean to assume.

awg.surface: She denied it three times. 'What? No. I'm not — no.'
awg.actual: Three denials. One would be enough if it were true. Three means it's the most true thing about her. The overcorrection reveals the core: she's a comedian who's terrified of being a comedian. The denial is louder than any admission would be.
awg.tell: She broke character. The smooth, confident gas station comedian stuttered. The stutter is the real Marcus — the version without the bit.
awg.recommendation: Mirror her denial with your own. Show her you understand hiding from the thing you want most, because you're doing the same thing. Don't reassure — relate.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your talented friend works too. The one who says 'I'm not that good' about the thing they're clearly great at. The denial isn't modesty — it's terror of being seen wanting something.
awg.closer: Are We Good counts the denials.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Don't — don't do that. Don't say it like you know.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She flinched. Actual physical flinch. Sincerity without the comedy buffer hits her like a bright light hits someone who's been in the dark.

options.text: You're right. I don't know. But I know the hot dog contest is going to be incredible.

awg.surface: Immediate response. No comic delay. No riff. Just 'don't.'
awg.actual: The speed tells you everything. Marcus's humor has a one-to-two-second build. Responses faster than that are pre-comedic — they come from below the performance. 'Don't' at that speed is pure flinch reflex. You touched a nerve that doesn't have a joke wrapped around it yet.
awg.tell: Physical flinch. Bodies don't lie. Her comedy persona lives in her voice. The flinch lives in her body. The body overruled the voice.
awg.recommendation: Redirect to safe ground. Put the joke back. Give her the comedy buffer she needs to come down from the exposure. She'll come back to sincerity when she's ready — on her timeline, not yours.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your deflecting friend works too. When you say something too real and they go 'stop,' they mean 'I heard you and it landed and I need thirty seconds to not cry.' Give them the thirty seconds.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows when 'don't' means 'too close.'

dialogue_tree.npc_line: If you make it to Coney Island, save me a seat on the boardwalk. July 5th I'll tell you how the open mic went. Or I'll lie about it. Either way, good story.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's inviting you to her future. In Marcus-language, that's a marriage proposal.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Safe travels, hot dog pilgrim. May your buns be warm and your mustard plentiful.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: A blessing. Delivered as a joke. Meaning every word.

real.description: Marcus has dropped the bit. Not all of it — she'll never drop all of it. But the ratio has shifted. More real, less material. She's scared of the open mic. She's scared of you seeing that she's scared. She's scared of being ordinary.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I have a question and I need you to answer it like a person, not like a motivational poster.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's asking for sincerity. From Marcus, this is like a cat asking to be held. Rare. Fragile. Do not fumble it.

options.text: Okay. Person mode. Go.
I promise no posters. Maybe a small pamphlet at most.

awg.surface: She said 'answer it like a person, not like a motivational poster.'
awg.actual: She's distinguishing between real and performed encouragement. She's heard 'you can do it!' before — it bounces off. She needs you to be honest, even if honest isn't optimistic. The fact that she specified 'like a person' means she trusts you to be one.
awg.tell: She pre-empted the response she doesn't want. That means she's gotten that response before and it failed her. She's coaching you on how to help her.
awg.recommendation: Be honest. If she's asking for 'person mode,' give her person mode. A small joke at the edges is fine — she needs the bridge — but the core answer has to be real.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your anxious friend works too. 'Don't just say it'll be fine' means 'I need you to take my fear seriously before I can put it down.'
awg.closer: Are We Good hears the coaching inside the question.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: What if I get up there and I'm just... fine? Not bad. Not good. Just ordinary. What if that's worse than bombing?
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: There it is. The thing underneath all the jokes. Not fear of failure — fear of mediocrity. Fear that the thing she's built her whole identity around is just... average.

options.text: Ordinary is just the word scared people use for 'beginning.' Nobody's good the first time. They're just brave enough to be bad.
I'm crossing a continent for a hot dog contest. We're both past 'ordinary.'
You won't be ordinary. You're too talented.

awg.surface: She said 'what if I'm just fine?' Not 'what if I bomb.'
awg.actual: The absent fear tells you the real fear. She didn't say 'what if I'm terrible' — she can handle terrible. Terrible is comedy material. 'Fine' is the nightmare because 'fine' has no punchline. 'Fine' means she's not special. And being special is the only thing standing between Marcus and whoever she was before the jokes started.
awg.tell: She said 'worse than bombing.' She's ranked the fears. Bombing is survivable. Ordinary is not. The hierarchy reveals the wound.
awg.recommendation: Don't reassure. Reframe. 'Ordinary' isn't the actual risk — 'beginning' is. She's conflating first attempt with final verdict. Separate them for her.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your perfectionist friend works too. They'd rather not try than try and be average. 'What if I'm just okay?' is the question that keeps people on the couch instead of the stage.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears the fear that hides behind the better fear.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I left Howard after one semester. Full ride. Did I ever tell you that? No. Because it's not funny. It's just a thing I did because I was afraid of finding out I was regular.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The notebook is in her hand now. Not the back pocket. Her hand. She's holding it like evidence.

options.text: You left because you were afraid. And now you're signing up for an open mic. That's not regular, Marcus. That's the opposite of regular.
Can I hear one? From the notebook?

awg.surface: She told you about Howard. Unprompted. In a gas station.
awg.actual: She's connecting the dots for you — Howard, the gas station, the open mic, the fear. She's narrating her own arc because she finally has an audience she trusts enough to tell the non-funny version. The topic architecture shifted from comedy to autobiography. For Marcus, autobiography is the hardest bit.
awg.tell: The notebook is in her hand. Not hidden. Visible. The hiding place became a holding place. The object changed meaning without changing position.
awg.recommendation: Either honor the confession with a reframe, or honor the craft by asking to hear it. Both say 'I see you.' Different doors to the same room.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your brave friend works too. They don't announce the brave thing in advance. They just do it. And then they tell you about it after, shaking, in a gas station at 2pm.
awg.closer: Are We Good sees the notebook come out of the pocket.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: See, that's a motivational poster. I asked you not to do that.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's not angry. She's disappointed. Which is worse.

options.text: You're right. Okay. Real answer: I don't know if you'll be good. I know you'll be there. That's the hard part.

awg.surface: She referenced her earlier instruction — 'I asked you not to do that.'
awg.actual: She's holding you to what you agreed to. Consistency matters with humor-gated people because they've been let down by people who promise 'real' and deliver 'nice.' 'You're too talented' isn't real — it's nice. And nice is the thing Marcus trusts least.
awg.tell: She reminded you of the rule. The callback structure — referencing something from earlier — is how Marcus processes disappointment. Even her hurt comes out as a bit.
awg.recommendation: Correct course immediately. Admit you went poster. Give the real answer — the uncertain, honest, non-optimistic-but-true answer. She'd rather hear 'I don't know' than 'you'll be great.'
awg.bridge_line: This is how your bullshit-detector friend works too. They asked for real and you gave them Hallmark. They'll forgive it once if you catch yourself. Twice and you're filed under 'not safe.'
awg.closer: Are We Good catches the callback to the broken promise.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: July 4th, you eat hot dogs. July 5th, I eat microphone. We'll compare notes. I'll be the one throwing up from nerves. You'll be the one throwing up from hot dogs. It'll be beautiful.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's crying. Just a little. She'll deny it. She'll say it's allergies. In a gas station. In the middle of nowhere. Allergies.

name: Elena
role: Motel cleaning staff who has been in the country for twelve years and is invisible in exactly the way she needs to be
closes_when: One big gesture instead of small consistent ones
appearance: Cleaning cart always within arm's reach. Hair net even when off shift — habit. Hands that are simultaneously the cleanest and most worn things in any room. A small gold cross necklace that she touches when she's thinking, not praying.
motivation: Has been saving for twelve years to bring her two sons from Tegucigalpa. She's $800 short. She will not ask for help. She will not take shortcuts. She will get there on schedule.
secret: She owns the motel. Technically. The previous owner signed it over to her in his will because she was the only one who showed up to work every day for eight years. She hasn't filed the paperwork because filing it means becoming visible.

observer.description: Elena sees you before you see her. She's been invisible for twelve years — she knows how to watch without being watched. She won't engage first. She'll assess your consistency through action, not words.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Room's not ready yet. Twenty minutes.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: The room has been ready for two hours. She wants to see if you can wait.

options.text: No problem. I'll be right here.
Can you hurry? I really need to rest.
Twenty minutes is fine. Take your time — I know this work isn't easy.
Here — let me help you with those towels while I wait.

awg.surface: She said 'twenty minutes' about a room that's already ready.
awg.actual: The delay is a calibration tool. Consistency-required people don't trust first impressions — they trust patterns. By creating a wait, she's collecting your first data point. How you handle twenty minutes of nothing tells her more than twenty minutes of conversation.
awg.tell: She's still working while you wait. Not avoiding you — observing you through peripheral vision while pushing the cleaning cart. She's watching whether your patience changes when you think she's not looking.
awg.recommendation: Wait. Really wait. Don't fidget. Don't check your phone conspicuously. Don't complain to the air. The waiting IS the conversation. Pass this test and the next one gets easier.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your long-term partner works too. They don't trust the proposal — they trust the ten thousand mornings you made coffee without being asked. Consistency is the only love language they believe.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows the twenty minutes was always a test.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Room 7. Ice machine is at the end of the hall. It works on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She's giving you the real schedule, not the posted one. That's a small gift from someone who deals in small gifts.

options.text: Thank you. I'll remember — Tuesdays and Thursdays.
Thanks. Hey, is there anything else I should know about this place?

awg.surface: She gave you the ice machine schedule without being asked.
awg.actual: Unrequested useful information is Elena's opening bid. She doesn't give compliments or warmth — she gives utility. 'The ice machine works on Tuesdays and Thursdays' is Elena saying 'I've decided you might deserve to know how things actually work here.' The upgrade from posted schedule to real schedule is trust.
awg.tell: She specified days. Precision is Elena's affection. Vague help is polite. Specific help is personal.
awg.recommendation: Remember the detail. Repeat it back. Next time you see her, mention Tuesday ice. Consistency-required receivers track what you remember because memory proves attention, and attention over time proves care.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your reliable coworker works too. They don't say 'I've got your back.' They just always have your back. And they notice whether you notice.
awg.closer: Are We Good tracks the unrequested intel as trust.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Twenty minutes.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: Same words. Same tone. Nothing changed except everything. The repetition is the wall.

options.text: Sorry. You're right. Twenty minutes. I'll wait.
Fine.

awg.surface: She repeated 'twenty minutes' exactly — same words, same tone.
awg.actual: The exact repetition is the message. She didn't escalate. She didn't accommodate. She just repeated. For consistency-required receivers, repeating themselves IS the boundary. They don't negotiate. They don't explain. They wait for you to meet the standard they've already set.
awg.tell: Nothing in her body language changed. Not even the volume. The immovability IS the communication.
awg.recommendation: Correct yourself. Apologize briefly (not extensively — extensive apologies are performance). Then wait the twenty minutes without another word. Data point one was bad. Data point two needs to be clean.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your quiet authority figure works too. They don't raise their voice. They just repeat themselves. And somehow the repetition is louder than any shout.
awg.closer: Are We Good hears the wall inside the repetition.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: I don't need help with the towels.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She does need help with the towels. She also needs you to not make a show of it. The offer was too big, too fast.

options.text: Of course. Sorry. I'll wait over here.
Just trying to help. Let me know if you change your mind.

awg.surface: She refused help. Firmly.
awg.actual: The refusal isn't about the towels. It's about the gesture. Consistency-required receivers distrust large first offers because large first offers are easy. Anyone can help once. She needs someone who shows up small, repeatedly, without fanfare. The towel offer was too much too soon — it looked like a transaction, not a pattern.
awg.tell: She said 'I don't need help' — emphasis on 'I.' She's distinguishing between the towels (which need carrying) and herself (who doesn't need saving).
awg.recommendation: Back off. Way off. Then next time, do something small without asking. Leave a dollar tip on the nightstand. Close the door quietly. These are the data points Elena collects.
awg.bridge_line: This is how your independent friend works too. They don't want your grand rescue. They want you to text 'hey' every Tuesday without being asked. The small consistent thing is worth more than the big one-time thing.
awg.closer: Are We Good knows the towels weren't the point.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Checkout is at 11. But if you leave the key on the desk, I won't charge for late.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: A small rule bent. From Elena, that's a handshake.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Checkout is at 11.
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: No bend. No extra information. You got the posted schedule, not the real one.

measuring.description: Elena remembers you. She's comparing this version of you to the last one. Consistency means same person, every time. Not better — same.

dialogue_tree.npc_line: Room 7 again?
dialogue_tree.narrator_line: She remembers the room number. She won't remember your name for two more encounters. Rooms are facts. Names are promises.

options.text: If it's available. I liked the view of the parking lot. Very inspirational.
Elena. It's good to see you.
Elena, I brought you something. [Gift]

awg.surface: She said 'Room 7 again?' — she remembered the room.
awg.actual: She stored a fact about you. Not a feeling, not a name — a room number. For consistency-required receivers, facts are the foundation. She's building a file on you, and 'Room 7' is the first entry. She'll add to it only if you keep matching the pattern.
awg.tell: Question mark at the end. She's checking if you're consistent — do you want the same thing you wanted last time? Same request = same person = safe.
awg.recommendation: Be the same. Not grander, not different, not better. The same. Order Room 7. Wait patiently. Leave a tip. The pattern is the proof.
